input_signals.name: AccrualBuildupDecayingProfit
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(wcap, che), 1), at), 1)), RANK(NEG(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 5), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The lowest-quality accounting state is a firm accumulating non-cash working capital while its multi-year gross profitability is deteriorating, because the accrual buildup is then propping up a declining business rather than funding real expansion, and these accruals must be written down.
input_signals.reasoning: Replacing the signed product with a product of two [0,1] ranks removes the sign ambiguity the critic identified: the extreme value of the signal is now unambiguously the high-accrual, falling-profitability quadrant rather than a mixture of two opposite quadrants. The interaction is genuine because either leg alone is unremarkable — accrual buildup accompanied by improving gross profitability, or profit decline without accrual accumulation, both score near the middle.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( winsor( ratio( delta( sub( wcap, che ), 1 ), at ), 1 ) ), rank( neg( winsor( trend( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), 5 ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ChronicAccrualFallingTurnover
input_signals.hypothesis: Operating efficiency, not profitability, is the quality dimension that validates working-capital accruals: a firm that has accumulated working capital for three consecutive years while its asset turnover deteriorates is building operating assets that generate progressively less revenue, and those assets must eventually be written down.
input_signals.reasoning: Single-year accruals mean-revert, so cumulating three years isolates chronic rather than transitory accumulation, and asset turnover is an efficiency measure economically distinct from the gross-profitability trend already tested. This distinguishes whether the winning mechanism is about margin decay or about the productivity of the assets the accruals create.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( winsor( ts_sum( ratio( delta( sub( wcap, che ), 1 ), at ), 3 ), 1 ) ), rank( neg( winsor( trend( ratio( sale, at ), 5 ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: DebtFinancedAccrualBuildup
input_signals.hypothesis: Working-capital accruals funded by new long-term borrowing are qualitatively different from those funded internally: the firm is not converting reported profit into operating assets but is borrowing to carry receivables and inventory it cannot finance from operations, and this is a leading indicator of forced liquidation of those accruals.
input_signals.reasoning: The quality dimension here is the funding source of the accrual rather than the profitability that accompanies it, a channel untested in the archive and one that explains why some high-accrual firms reverse violently while others do not. It also directly repairs the weak `PayablesStretchLeverageTrap` idea by replacing a static leverage level with the flow of new debt that actually finances the current-period accrual.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( winsor( ratio( delta( sub( wcap, che ), 1 ), at ), 1 ) ), rank( winsor( ratio( delta( dltt, 1 ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: IndustryNeutralChronicAccrualDecay
input_signals.hypothesis: Working-capital intensity and asset turnover are structurally determined by industry (retailers turn assets several times, utilities do not), so the economically meaningful comparison is within industry; the accrual-quality interaction should be sharper once industry composition is removed from both legs.
input_signals.reasoning: The best archive signal may be partly loading on a static industry bet, which the FF5 model does not span and which makes the portfolio composition unstable over time. Ranking both legs within industry tests whether the mechanism is a genuine firm-level accounting-quality effect and should improve the reliability of the alpha t-stat even if the raw alpha shrinks somewhat.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ts_sum( ratio( delta( sub( wcap, che ), 1 ), at ), 3 ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( neg( winsor( trend( ratio( sale, at ), 5 ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualAccelerationTurnoverDecay
input_signals.hypothesis: A sudden acceleration in operating-capital accumulation is more diagnostic than its level or its steady growth, because a firm whose working capital is not merely growing but growing at an increasing rate while its asset productivity falls has lost control of collections and inventory rather than made a deliberate investment.
input_signals.reasoning: All archive accrual legs are levels, first differences, or three-year sums; the second difference is a distinct temporal concept that captures a regime break in working-capital management rather than a gradual build. Pairing it with the best-performing quality conditioner isolates whether the accrual anomaly here is about the stock accumulated or about the rate of deterioration.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( accel( ratio( sub( wcap, che ), at ) ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( neg( winsor( trend( ratio( sale, at ), 5 ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: CashBackedImprovingProductivity
input_signals.hypothesis: The mirror of the archive's best result should hold on the long side: firms that have generated three years of revenue growth without absorbing capital into receivables and inventory, while their asset productivity improves, are running genuinely cash-backed operations and are systematically underpriced.
input_signals.reasoning: Every strong archive signal is a corner product whose short leg is sharply defined while the long leg pools the entire remaining cross-section, so we do not yet know whether the −4.7% alpha is earned by shorting accrual-bloated decliners or by holding cash-efficient improvers. This mirror corner isolates the long side directly and is the first test of the task's stated economic story from the positive direction, and its result determines whether a final consolidated signal should be built as a two-sided sort or as a short-side screen.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( neg( winsor( ts_sum( ratio( delta( sub( wcap, che ), 1 ), at ), 3 ), 1 ) ) ), ind_rank( winsor( trend( ratio( sale, at ), 5 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: TripleCleanGrowthPersistence
input_signals.hypothesis: Genuinely durable cash earnings require three simultaneous conditions — revenue growth not funded by working capital, rising asset productivity, and an unbroken record of profitability — and firms satisfying all three are the cleanest identification of the task's economic story.
input_signals.reasoning: Loss frequency proved to be an economically independent conditioner on the short side (alpha −3.8%, t = −4.24) despite being nearly uncorrelated with turnover trends, so adding it as a third conjunct should sharpen the long leg where the FMB evidence is concentrated rather than merely reweighting existing information. The risk is over-conditioning into a thin corner, which the coverage and Sharpe diagnostics will reveal directly.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( mul( ind_rank( neg( winsor( ts_sum( ratio( delta( sub( wcap, che ), 1 ), at ), 3 ), 1 ) ) ), ind_rank( winsor( trend( ratio( sale, at ), 5 ), 1 ) ) ), ind_rank( ma( indicator( ni, 0 ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: CashBuildWithProfitImprovement
input_signals.hypothesis: The most direct evidence that reported profitability improvement is real is that the cash balance grows alongside it; firms whose gross profitability is trending up while cash per dollar of sales also rises are converting accounting gains into liquid resources rather than into soft operating assets.
input_signals.reasoning: The earlier cash-stock test failed on the short side, where falling cash is hopelessly confounded by investment and buybacks, but on the long side the confound works in our favor — accumulating cash while profitability improves cannot be manufactured by accrual choices. Scaling by sales rather than assets makes the measure comparable for asset-light firms and avoids the mechanical link to the asset base used in the profitability leg.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( delta( ratio( che, sale ), 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( winsor( trend( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), 5 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: CleanGrowthVersusFragileBloat
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(WINSOR(TS_SUM(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(wcap, che), 1), at), 3), 1))), IND_RANK(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(sale, at), 5), 1))), NEG(MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(TS_SUM(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(wcap, che), 1), at), 3), 1)), IND_RANK(NEG(WINSOR(TS_MIN(RATIO(ni, at), 5), 1))))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The bullish state and the bearish state are defined by different quality conditions: clean growth is identified by rising asset productivity without working-capital absorption, while impairment risk is identified by working-capital accumulation in firms with no profitability floor, so a two-sided signal must use the conditioner appropriate to each side.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic's algebra is correct — complementary corners built on the *same* conditioner collapse to the linear rank difference — so this version pairs the long corner with the turnover trend (where the archive's cross-sectional slope was strongest, fmb +4.86) and the short corner with the five-year worst-case ROA (a fragility measure that is not the complement of a turnover trend), which prevents any algebraic cancellation. The construction is genuinely two-sided and nonlinear because the two conditioners are economically and statistically distinct, so both corner products survive the sum.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( mul( ind_rank( neg( winsor( ts_sum( ratio( delta( sub( wcap, che ), 1 ), at ), 3 ), 1 ) ) ), ind_rank( winsor( trend( ratio( sale, at ), 5 ), 1 ) ) ), neg( mul( ind_rank( winsor( ts_sum( ratio( delta( sub( wcap, che ), 1 ), at ), 3 ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( neg( winsor( ts_min( ratio( ni, at ), 5 ), 1 ) ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: SupplierFinancedMarginGain
input_signals.hypothesis: Extending payables is a sign of bargaining power rather than distress when it occurs alongside a multi-year improvement in gross profitability: such a firm is financing its operating cycle with free supplier credit while its economics improve, which is the highest-quality form of negative working capital.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic is right that the sign was backwards — an increase in payables mechanically lowers accruals and the archive's own payables test produced a positive FMB slope against a negative prior — so this version reverses the direction and supplies the missing conditioning that distinguishes bargaining power from financing strain. The interaction is essential because payables growth alone is ambiguous, and only its coincidence with improving profitability identifies supplier credit as a competitive advantage rather than a liquidity symptom.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( apalch, at ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( winsor( trend( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), 5 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: WorkingCapitalCashReleaseWithMarginGain
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(apalch, ADD(recch, invch)), sale), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 5), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm that releases cash from its entire operating cycle — collecting receivables faster, carrying less inventory, and financing more from suppliers — while its gross profitability is simultaneously improving has genuinely tightened its operations, whereas the same cash release with deteriorating margins is asset liquidation by a shrinking business.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the single-component inventory test, which the critic correctly identified as the published Abarbanell–Bushee and Thomas–Zhang inventory anomaly, with the *net* cash conversion cycle assembled from all three trade-cycle lines of the cash-flow statement, where the sign convention already makes positive values cash-releasing. The profitability trend is not decorative: it is what separates efficiency-driven working-capital release from distress-driven liquidation, which is exactly the ambiguity that makes single-component inventory or receivable signals unstable.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( add( apalch, add( recch, invch ) ), sale ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( winsor( trend( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), 5 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: ConservativeDepreciationCleanAccruals
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms that depreciate aggressively relative to industry peers while refusing to inflate working capital are running conservative accounting on both the long-lived asset side and the operating cycle side, which understates current earnings and produces systematically positive future earnings surprises.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's only depreciation test looked for the *abuse* of under-depreciation and found nothing (alpha −0.2%), but the conservatism story runs the other way and has never been tested: high depreciation intensity depresses reported income today without touching cash. Industry ranking is essential here because depreciation intensity is dominated by capital intensity, and pairing it with the clean-accrual leg distinguishes genuine conservatism from mere asset-heaviness.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( neg( winsor( ts_sum( ratio( delta( sub( wcap, che ), 1 ), at ), 3 ), 1 ) ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ratio( dpc, sale ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: SelfFundedHistoryCleanAccruals
input_signals.hypothesis: A high ratio of retained earnings to book equity means the firm's capital base was built from realized profits rather than issued securities, and when such a self-funded firm is currently not absorbing cash into working capital, its reported earnings have been validated both historically and contemporaneously.
input_signals.reasoning: Every quality conditioner tested so far is either a five-year trend, a volatility, or a recent count; the retained-earnings share of equity is a cumulative lifetime record of cash-generating capacity that is nearly free of estimation noise and orthogonal to short-window trend measures. The interaction matters because mature self-funded firms with rising working capital are precisely the ones whose historical record lulls investors into ignoring current accrual deterioration.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( neg( winsor( ts_sum( ratio( delta( sub( wcap, che ), 1 ), at ), 3 ), 1 ) ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ratio( re, ceq ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: CashValidatedLongVersusDecayShort
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(che, sale), 1), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 5), 1))), NEG(MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(TS_SUM(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(wcap, che), 1), at), 3), 1)), IND_RANK(NEG(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(sale, at), 5), 1))))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The two tails are identified by different accounting evidence: on the long side, improving profitability is credible only when the cash balance is visibly building, while on the short side, working-capital accumulation is dangerous only when the productivity of the asset base is falling — so the bullish screen should be cash-based and the bearish screen operating-capital-based.
input_signals.reasoning: This deliberately joins the archive's two diagnostic opposites rather than reshuffling one family: the cash-build corner produced a strong cross-sectional slope (fmb +3.54) with no alpha, while the accrual-decay corner produced the archive's largest alpha (−4.7%, t = −5.11) with a weaker slope, and the two rest on completely disjoint inputs (cash stock and gross margin versus working-capital flow and asset turnover). Because no leg is the complement of any other, the composite cannot collapse to a linear rank difference, and it targets the joint FMB-plus-alpha objective by construction.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( mul( ind_rank( winsor( delta( ratio( che, sale ), 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( winsor( trend( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), 5 ), 1 ) ) ), neg( mul( ind_rank( winsor( ts_sum( ratio( delta( sub( wcap, che ), 1 ), at ), 3 ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( neg( winsor( trend( ratio( sale, at ), 5 ), 1 ) ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: OperatingTighteningRegime
input_signals.hypothesis: What identifies a genuine operational tightening is a firm reaching the lowest operating-capital intensity and the highest asset productivity of its own five-year history simultaneously — a regime shift relative to how the firm itself has always run, not a position in the cross-sectional distribution.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic's algebra is correct that flipping cross-sectional ranks on both legs of an existing signal differs only by linear terms, so this version replaces both legs with within-firm historical percentiles, which are not affine transformations of the cross-sectional ranks and carry information about firm-specific regime change rather than peer position. Industry-ranking the two within-firm states afterwards keeps the comparison peer-relative while the underlying variation is entirely new to the archive.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( neg( ts_rank( ratio( sub( wcap, che ), sale ), 5 ) ) ), ind_rank( ts_rank( ratio( sale, at ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: PredictableAccrualsSustainedProfit
input_signals.hypothesis: Earnings quality depends on how *predictable* a firm's accruals are, not only on their level: a firm whose working-capital requirement varies little from year to year while it sustains high gross profitability has an operating cycle that maps reliably into cash, so its reported income requires little estimation and rarely reverses.
input_signals.reasoning: Every accrual leg in the archive measures magnitude — level, flow, cumulative flow, acceleration, or firm-history position — and none measures the second moment, yet accrual volatility is the core of the accounting literature's own definition of accrual quality. Pairing it with sustained gross profitability rather than a trend distinguishes stable, cash-converting business models from firms that are merely quiet because they are stagnant.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( neg( winsor( vol( ratio( delta( sub( wcap, che ), 1 ), at ), 5 ), 1 ) ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ma( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), 3 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: TurnoverFreeTwoSidedQuality
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(che, sale), 1), 1)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 5), 1))), NEG(MUL(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(wcap, che), sale), 1)), IND_RANK(NEG(WINSOR(TS_MIN(RATIO(ni, at), 5), 1))))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The accrual-quality interaction should survive without any reference to asset turnover: cash accumulation alongside margin improvement identifies genuine performance on one side, and soft-asset bloat in firms with no profitability floor identifies impairment risk on the other.
input_signals.reasoning: Asset turnover appears in nearly every strong archive signal, which raises the concern that the results are a repackaged Soliman-style turnover effect rather than an accruals-times-quality interaction. Removing turnover entirely from both corners is the cleanest robustness test available, and a materially positive result would establish the mechanism as genuinely about cash backing rather than about asset productivity.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( mul( ind_rank( winsor( delta( ratio( che, sale ), 1 ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( winsor( trend( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), 5 ), 1 ) ) ), neg( mul( ind_rank( winsor( ratio( sub( wcap, che ), sale ), 1 ) ), ind_rank( neg( winsor( ts_min( ratio( ni, at ), 5 ), 1 ) ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: RareAccrualYearsSustainedProfit
input_signals.hypothesis: What distinguishes cash-backed performance is the *frequency* with which a firm needs to absorb cash into working capital, not the size of any one year's absorption: a firm that has increased non-cash working capital in only one or two of the past five years while sustaining high gross profitability funds its profits from operations as a matter of policy rather than by chance.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive has measured the accrual leg only by magnitude — level, flow, cumulative flow, acceleration, volatility, firm-history position — and never by the count of accruing years, which is the accrual-side analogue of the loss-frequency conditioner that produced a −3.8% alpha with t = −4.24. A frequency measure is robust to the single large outlier years that dominate magnitude measures, and pairing it with a three-year average gross profitability level (rather than a trend) tests policy consistency on both sides of the interaction.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( neg( ma( indicator( delta( sub( wcap, che ), 1 ), 0 ), 5 ) ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ma( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), 3 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: TaxConfirmedCleanAccruals
input_signals.hypothesis: Tax authorities are an adversarial third party who do not accept accrual discretion, so a rising tax obligation per dollar of sales is independent confirmation that taxable income genuinely grew; combined with three years of growth that did not absorb working capital, it means reported earnings have been validated by an outside party with the power to audit them.
input_signals.reasoning: This repairs a proposal that failed validation last round for lacking a quality-exclusive variable by deflating the tax accrual with sales rather than assets, and it introduces the only validator in the archive drawn from a reporting system outside the financial statements themselves. The archive's single tax test was a standalone rank difference (fmb +0.81, correct sign but weak); conditioning it on the clean-accrual state asks the sharper question of whether tax confirmation adds information precisely where accrual evidence is already favorable.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( neg( winsor( ts_sum( ratio( delta( sub( wcap, che ), 1 ), at ), 3 ), 1 ) ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ratio( delta( txp, 1 ), sale ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: DualPolicyConsistency
input_signals.hypothesis: Durable cash earnings are a matter of repeated behavior on both sides of the interaction: a firm that rarely absorbs cash into working capital and that improves its gross profitability in most years is running a consistently disciplined operation, and consistency of direction is more informative than the size of any single year's change.
input_signals.reasoning: Every quality conditioner in the archive is a magnitude — a trend slope, a volatility, a minimum, or a level — whereas the accrual side has just shown that a simple count of favorable years dominates its magnitude analogues on cross-sectional evidence. This tests whether the same robustness argument transfers to the quality leg, which would be a substantively different finding about how earnings quality should be measured rather than another recombination of existing components.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( neg( ma( indicator( delta( sub( wcap, che ), 1 ), 0 ), 5 ) ) ), ind_rank( ma( indicator( delta( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), 1 ), 0 ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: CashAccumulationHabitProfitable
input_signals.hypothesis: The most direct evidence that profits are real is that the cash balance grows repeatedly: a firm whose cash-to-assets ratio has risen in most of the past five years while sustaining high gross profitability is banking its reported earnings rather than recycling them into soft assets or financing.
input_signals.reasoning: The single-year cash-change tests failed because Δcash is dominated by financing and investment activity, but a five-year count of cash-building years averages that noise away and isolates firms with a persistent tendency to accumulate liquidity. This applies the validated frequency logic to the cash stock rather than to working capital, testing whether the mechanism is about avoiding accruals or about visibly banking the cash — a distinction the archive has not yet resolved.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ma( indicator( delta( ratio( che, at ), 1 ), 0 ), 5 ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ma( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), 3 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: GrowthAdjustedAccrualHabit
input_signals.hypothesis: A rise in non-cash working capital is mechanical for any growing firm, so the informative event is not that working capital increased but that it increased *faster than sales*; counting the years in which operating-capital intensity per dollar of revenue deteriorated isolates genuine loss of cash discipline from ordinary expansion.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's best signal counts raw working-capital increases, which mechanically penalizes fast-growing firms and rewards stagnant ones, so scale-adjusting the event inside the indicator is an economic correction rather than a recombination of legs — it changes which firms trigger the count, not merely how the count is weighted. Pairing it with sustained gross profitability keeps the quality leg identical to the archive's best result so the improvement in the accrual event definition can be read cleanly.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( neg( ma( indicator( delta( ratio( sub( wcap, che ), sale ), 1 ), 0 ), 5 ) ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ma( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), 3 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: BalanceSheetMigrationToCash
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(MA(INDICATOR(SUB(DELTA(RATIO(che, sale), 1), DELTA(RATIO(SUB(wcap, che), sale), 1)), 0), 5)), IND_RANK(WINSOR(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 3), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Earnings quality shows up as a migration in the composition of the balance sheet: firms that repeatedly shift their current assets from receivables and inventory toward cash are converting reported profit into the one asset that cannot be re-estimated, and when this happens alongside sustained gross profitability it is evidence of genuine cash generation rather than shrinkage.
input_signals.reasoning: This is not another arrangement of existing corners: the accrual leg counts years in which cash intensity grew *faster than* soft operating-capital intensity, a relative-composition event that no archive signal measures, and which sidesteps the financing contamination that killed the raw Δcash tests because both terms are affected by financing in the same direction. The profitability conditioner is essential to rule out the liquidation interpretation, in which cash rises simply because the business is being wound down.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ma( indicator( sub( delta( ratio( che, sale ), 1 ), delta( ratio( sub( wcap, che ), sale ), 1 ) ), 0 ), 5 ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ma( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), 3 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: RepeatedTaxConfirmation
input_signals.hypothesis: Repeated increases in taxes payable per dollar of sales mean an adversarial third party has confirmed the firm's income growth year after year, and a firm that earns this confirmation repeatedly while rarely absorbing cash into working capital has reported earnings validated both by the tax authority and by its own operating cycle.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the depreciation channel, which the critic correctly argued is confounded by capex cycles and falling sales and which the archive has twice shown to carry little content, in favor of the tax validator that did work (alpha +2.0%, t = +2.42) but was measured as a single lumpy annual change. Taxes payable is a notoriously lumpy item, so recasting it as a five-year frequency of confirmation events applies the same robustness logic that lifted the accrual leg from a t of −1.4 in magnitude form to +5.24 in count form.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( neg( ma( indicator( delta( sub( wcap, che ), 1 ), 0 ), 5 ) ) ), ind_rank( ma( indicator( delta( ratio( txp, sale ), 1 ), 0 ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: CleanHabitDualQualityValidation
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(MA(INDICATOR(DELTA(SUB(wcap, che), 1), 0), 5))), IND_RANK(SUMRANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 3), TS_MIN(RATIO(ni, at), 5))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm's earnings are durable only if it is both highly profitable on average and never deeply unprofitable in any single year, so the quality side of the interaction should combine the profitability level with the profitability floor rather than relying on either alone.
input_signals.reasoning: The gross-profitability level and the worst-case ROA capture different failure modes — thin margins versus episodic collapse — and each has independently conditioned successful archive signals, but they have never been combined into a single validated quality state before being crossed with the accrual leg. Ranking the two quality measures jointly inside SUMRANK avoids the tie-heavy, lumpy portfolios produced when a six-valued count is used on both sides of the product.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( neg( ma( indicator( delta( sub( wcap, che ), 1 ), 0 ), 5 ) ) ), ind_rank( sumrank( ma( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), 3 ), ts_min( ratio( ni, at ), 5 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: WorstYearAccrualDisciplineProfit
input_signals.hypothesis: Operating discipline is defined by a firm's worst year, not its average: a company whose largest single-year absorption of cash into working capital over five years was still modest has an operating model that never loses control of collections and inventory, and when this is combined with sustained gross profitability the reported earnings are structurally cash-backed.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive has measured the accrual leg as a level, a one-year flow, a three-year sum, an acceleration, a volatility, a within-firm percentile and a frequency count, but never as the maximum of the annual distribution, which is the statistic that actually determines whether the firm ever had a control failure. It is also continuous rather than six-valued, so it should deliver the count leg's robustness to the average year while restoring the fine portfolio breakpoints that the count encoding sacrifices — directly addressing the granularity problem seen on the short side.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( neg( winsor( ts_max( ratio( delta( sub( wcap, che ), 1 ), at ), 5 ), 1 ) ) ), ind_rank( winsor( ma( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), 3 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: ImprovingAccrualDisciplineProfit
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(SUB(MA(INDICATOR(DELTA(SUB(wcap, che), 1), 0), 5), MA(INDICATOR(DELTA(SUB(wcap, che), 1), 0), 3))), IND_RANK(WINSOR(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 3), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: What predicts returns is not the level of a firm's accrual habit but its change: a company whose recent three-year frequency of working-capital absorption is lower than its five-year frequency is actively tightening its operating cycle, and that improvement in discipline is not yet reflected in reported earnings.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic is right that swapping one window for another is a hyperparameter tweak, so this version uses both windows simultaneously as a contrast, which measures a second-order behavioral concept — the trajectory of accrual discipline — that no archive signal captures. It is economically distinct because a firm can have a poor five-year record and still be improving sharply, and such firms are exactly the ones a level-based habit measure would wrongly place on the short side.

input_signals.name: RetainedEarningsHabitCleanHabit
input_signals.hypothesis: Durable earnings should show up twice: repeatedly as additions to the retained-earnings base, proving that reported income survived into permanent equity rather than being reversed by later write-offs, and repeatedly as an absence of working-capital absorption, proving the income arrived as cash rather than as receivables and inventory.
input_signals.reasoning: This drops the cash-flow-minus-income comparison that the critic correctly identified as a sign-only restatement of the Sloan total-accrual measure and replaces it with a validator drawn from the equity account, where accounting reversals eventually surface as retained-earnings write-downs that no working-capital measure can see. Both legs are five-year frequencies of behavior rather than magnitudes, which follows the encoding that produced the archive's strongest cross-sectional evidence while keeping the two constructs economically independent — one is about the fate of past income, the other about the form of current income.
